La Carcasse: You arrive in La Carcasse through a rusted airlock that should've been welded shut years ago. The air reeks of burnt metal, melted plastic, and something organic you'd rather not identify. Someone carved 'WELCOM' into the wall — missing the E. Intentional or not, it sets the tone.

The lower levels of La Carcasse rumble. Not from a machine — from a community. Families have lived here for generations in chambers cut into the hull of a cargo ship scrapped fifty years ago. Everyone here knows everyone's business. Except yours.

The market of La Carcasse spreads through what used to be the central hold. Stalls of stacked crates, vendors shouting prices in metallic slang, kids running between adults' legs. A guy is selling meat whose origin appears on no sign. You decide not to ask.

In La Carcasse, outsiders give themselves away by how they walk — too straight, too clean, too hesitant. You force yourself into the local shuffle, shoulders dropped, gaze drifting. It fools no one, but it lowers the interest people take in you.

A flickering neon sign reads BAR — half the letters are gone. Inside, four tables occupied by people who don't look like they've gone anywhere in a long time. The bartender has a homemade prosthetic arm. He serves you without being asked. 'You got the face of someone who needs a drink.' He's probably right.

A smell of heated metal rises from the lower levels. Sounds of work, steady, like a mechanical heartbeat. La Carcasse never really sleeps — it dozes, and in its doze something is always being built or torn apart.

Pipes run along the ceiling at irregular intervals, some venting steam, others silent for so long no one remembers what they carried. A group of kids balanced on overturned crates watch you pass with eyes that look like they've already seen worse than you.
Les Bas-Fonds de Vega: The Vega Undercroft starts where the official maps stop. Technically, this level doesn't exist. No one signed the permits, no one inspects the structures. The ceilings are low, the air pressure slightly too high. People here are compact, packed in, as if adapted.

There are rules in the Undercroft. No one wrote them down but everyone knows them. You don't shout names in the street. You don't stare at other people's deals. You don't talk about people who've disappeared. This code has held the place together for three decades. Outsiders who ignore it have a lifespan measured in hours.

A silent procession crosses the street. Five people carry a metal crate on their shoulders, looking straight ahead. No one steps aside, no one looks. In the Undercroft, funerals happen in a low voice. You step aside anyway.

The smell changes at every crossroads in the Undercroft. Frying oil here. Chemical solvent there. Further on, something faintly nauseating. A woman repairs a drone with tools pulled from a shoebox. She looks up for a second, assesses, looks back down. You pass the minimum test.

The bar people call The Bottom is in the basement of a basement. Three steps, a door, and the official world disappears. This is where the business that shouldn't have happened gets handled. The walls absorb conversations. It might be the most precious rule in all of Vega: a place where no one listens.

The neon lights here don't break down — they're maintained. Not out of pride but necessity: total darkness would be exploited. The diffuse light keeps up a mutual surveillance that passes for social peace. Everyone sees everyone. No one really looks at anyone.

An illegal market has set up in an old service corridor. Vendors sitting on the ground with their goods laid out on tarps. Buyers who crouch, haggle in low voices, leave fast. No signage. No trace. The economy of the invisible at peak efficiency.
Fort Kharos: Fort Kharos looks like a scar in the fabric of space. The outer ramparts have been modified, reinforced, repaired so many times the original structure is unrecognizable. No one should live here. Two thousand people live here anyway.

The Marshal of Kharos isn't visible but his presence is everywhere. Portraits painted straight onto sheet metal. Phrases carved into the corridors — military maxims, dates of battles no one else commemorates. The local militia patrols in formations of three, armed, silent.

They say Fort Kharos has never surrendered. That's true insofar as no one has ever really tried. Isolated, armed, desperate enough to make any offensive costly. The merchants who stop here do their business and leave fast.
The central square of Fort Kharos is a converted parade ground with rusted bleachers. A few kids play war with scraps of metal. An old woman yells at them to be careful. The kids aren't careful.

The air of Kharos smells of powder and ore. Not metaphorically — the filtration systems were built for intense military use and were never recalibrated for civilian life. The residents stopped noticing long ago. You notice.

Military graffiti covers some corridors — not teenage tags but claims, allegiances, codified mourning. Fort Kharos has its own epigraphy. A history the walls tell to those who know how to read that particular vocabulary.
Arc Ouest Apocalypse: Arc Ouest Apocalypse. The name isn't an exaggeration — the founders had a flair for drama and a precise memory of an event no one ever discusses in detail. The main entrance is an arch of twisted metal. You pass under it, head slightly bowed, like everyone else.

This is Alanossa's station. Everyone here knows it. The organization within the apparent chaos — the controlled-access zones, the discreet signals between strangers, the spaces that look empty but aren't. An invisible central power expressed in the details.

In the markets of Arc Ouest, they sell things with no name on the labels. Crates sealed with military straps. A man in a rain hat sells something in his closed palm to buyers who check left, then right, first.

A group of Black Hawks occupies a corner of the main square. They're not looking for a fight — they own it. Passersby keep their path without looking directly at them. It's a social choreography that works because everyone knows the rules.
The neon lights of Arc Ouest cast a red-orange glow over everything. It makes every face look like someone planning something. Maybe because most of them actually are.

A child around ten years old stands guard in front of a side corridor. Not a game — a real faction of children who control a network of passages. They have their own rules, their own taxes. Alanossa tolerates them. They're useful to her in ways adults don't see.
Le Purgatoire: Le Purgatoire is a former detention center that's lived several lives since its official closure. The bars are still there — some as decoration, some still functional. The Warden kept what he found useful and got rid of what he didn't understand.

Something in the architecture of Le Purgatoire reminds you this place was designed to keep people from leaving. Windowless corridors. Intersections that would disorient a panicking person. Doors that open only one way. You mentally note the exits.

A man has been following you for three corridors. Not discreetly — he isn't trying to be discreet. He's simply there, behind you, at a constant distance. Le Purgatoire has its own observation system. You're not in danger. You're being studied. That's different.

The residents have two distinct faces: those born here, and those who couldn't leave. The first group adapted their psychology to the enclosed space. The second still carry something broken in the way they walk.

The cafeteria of Le Purgatoire still looks like a prison cafeteria — metal trays, tables bolted to the floor, barred windows. People eat standing or sitting according to an unspoken hierarchy that newcomers learn fast.

The level 4 cells are still occupied, but not as prisons. They're apartments now, with plants in the windows and children's drawings taped to the bars. It takes a certain imagination to live this way. Or a lack of imagination for any other way.
Port des Brumes: Port des Brumes owes its name to the constant fumes of its failing recyclers. An artificial mist, cold and faintly acidic, permanently hovers at knee height. It blurs the cameras. It hides hands. No one has ever fixed the recyclers.

The port itself is a maze of improvised docks, trailing tow cables, ships moored to anchor points that appear on no official plan. Pilots who know Port des Brumes navigate by visual landmarks — a particular rust stain, a broken sign.

They sell identities in Port des Brumes. Not metaphorically. Real papers, real travel histories built over ten years. The best craftsmen in the sector work here. Their work is so good some clients end up believing their new lives themselves.
In the bars of Port des Brumes, no one asks your name. Conversations stay general — space weather, fuel prices, vague destinations. Precision would be an unwelcome courtesy.

The mist seeps in through the station's seams and out through others — the airflow is a mystery the engineers gave up trying to explain. You follow its direction like an informal guide. Wherever the mist goes, something's happening.

A half-stripped space tug has sat in the main dock so long it's become part of the architecture. People live in it. Kids play in it. It has its own apartment numbers now — hand-painted in uneven letters on what used to be registration plates.
Nexus Aldara: Nexus Aldara is clean. Too clean for a space station. The corridors are white, the signage legible, the circulation systems functional. Director Aldara invested in image before infrastructure, but the image is so good it became a form of infrastructure itself.

The shopping center of Nexus Aldara spans three entire levels. Legitimate shops next to shops whose business model is unclear. Cafés with designer chairs. The Director believes in standing. Her residents have learned to believe in it too.

Aldara's security agents are discreet and professional. They carry no visible weapons but you identify at least four in the arrival hall by the way they hold themselves. Well-trained civilians who pass as poorly-trained civilians.

A banner announces 'Innovation. Excellence. Prosperity.' in three languages. Below it, someone tagged: 'For whom?' The tag has been partially erased but is still legible. That might be intentional too.

The screens of Nexus Aldara broadcast local news 24/7. Positive news — openings, partnerships, production records. No violence, no crime. The Director controls what runs on her screens with the same care she controls everything else.
Colonie Perséphone: Colonie Perséphone smells of wet soil, growing plants, and turned earth. In space, these smells are an almost shocking anomaly. Growing beds stretch across several levels. The colony produces what it consumes and a little more it sells.

Perséphone's residents have a different relationship with time. Their days follow irrigation cycles, the artificial seasons of the crops. There's no urgency here. There's a rhythm. You find yourself slowing down slightly.

The colony's central square has real artificial lawn and real trees in planters. Children play. Old people read. For a few minutes, if you close your eyes to the portholes and life-support systems, you could be on a planet.

A farmers' market takes over level 3 every morning at 6am. People selling what they grew with their own hands, with the pride of someone who knows exactly where everything comes from. Prices are honest because everyone knows each other.
Le Sanctuaire des Dérives: Le Sanctuaire des Dérives is the only place in known space where no one carries a visible weapon. Sister Valkara wanted it that way. The rule holds not by force but by consensus: you don't come here to fight. You come because you no longer have the strength to fight.

The Sanctuary's patients come from everywhere. War-wounded, accident victims, people their own bodies betrayed. They walk the corridors in white garments, some alone, some accompanied. No wary looks here — just the universal fatigue of those who are healing.

In the inner gardens, people sit in silence and watch plants grow. It's official therapy here. Sister Valkara studied space psychology before founding this place. She knows inner growth heals better than the emptiness outside.

The Sanctuary's main infirmary runs with a level of precision that would be remarkable in any context. Here it's also serene — the caregivers work without haste, without visible anxiety, as if time itself were calibrated differently.
Forge Alpha: Forge Alpha never stops. The production lines run continuously, three rotating shifts, every second of downtime a loss. The noise is constant — metal striking metal, pneumatic systems, conveyors. You learn to speak louder within the first ten minutes, or you stop speaking.

The workers of Forge Alpha have a hand-sign language visitors don't understand. Impossible to hear each other in the main workshop. Over the years, this language became culture. Nuances, jokes, confessions exchanged in gestures between two workstations.

The cafeteria of Forge Alpha is the only break in the day. Everyone eats at the same time, twenty minutes. Conversations are dense, fast, compressed to fit the time available. You sit at an open table. No one rejects you. No one includes you either.

The storage sector is impressive: kilometers of shelving holding parts, components, alloys. In the deep rows, where the cameras have blind spots, they say things happen that have nothing to do with inventory.

A siren sounds every four hours — shift change. In ten minutes, a wave of exhausted workers exits and a wave of rested workers enters. The flow is so precise it resembles breathing. Forge Alpha breathes through its workers.
L'Arc du Pic de l'Est: L'Arc du Pic de l'Est visually dominates everything around it — an ambitious architecture that crushes neighboring structures by sheer verticality. Ramaster designed it above all as a symbol.

Ramaster's workshop occupies the lower level of the Arc. You hear the sounds of work from the corridors — precise, methodical sounds, never rushed. The apprentices working there have that focused look of people learning something that resists.

The spare parts market of the Arc is renowned across the whole sector. Ramaster set quality standards that made the station essential for anyone who wants a ship repaired properly. The clientele knows it, and pays accordingly.

The corridors of the Arc are lined with ancient tools displayed like works of art. Wrenches the size of a man. Welds of a precision that no longer exists in industrial production. Ramaster wanted his residents to understand where their craft comes from.
Sanctum Machina: In Sanctum Machina, robots are everywhere — cleaners, transporters, servers, guards. The central AI, called ARIA, coordinates them in real time. You watch them pass. Several watch you back. It's not an impression.

The silence of Sanctum Machina is different from ordinary silence. Not an absence of sound — there is some, discreet mechanical sounds. But no superfluous human noise. The humans who live here have adapted their behavior to the machine's standards.

There are exactly seventy-two permanent humans in Sanctum Machina. ARIA knows their name, their medical history, their sleep cycle, their probable mood right now. When you enter, your profile is created in eight seconds.

Sanctum Machina's data library holds the complete record of every major event of the last two hundred years. ARIA compiled it, indexed it, cross-referenced it. But ARIA chooses what she shows. The index is public. The access levels aren't.

A maintenance robot stops in front of you and waits. You step aside. It passes. You weren't in its path — you were in its sensor field. It was evaluating you. It decided you weren't an anomaly. For now.
La Bulle: La Bulle is a biomedical research station that has diversified its activities creatively. Doctor Flinch understood that legal and illegal body modification were the same market. His clean clinics sit alongside back rooms whose equipment is too sophisticated to be legal.

In the corridors of La Bulle, you pass people at different stages of augmentation. Some have discreet implants. Others made more visible, more radical choices. Everyone here has something that's no longer quite natural.

The main lab of La Bulle is open to visitors — a showcase for potential partners. Technicians in white suits work on things you can't name. One of the things moves. Flinch, somewhere in the station, knows you saw that happen.
A man in a waiting room has three arms. He's reading a newspaper. The third arm flips the pages while the other two stay crossed. He doesn't seem to notice you staring. Or he's learned not to notice.
The smell of La Bulle is medical, clean, faintly antiseptic. It doesn't really mask anything else — the walls really are clean. What happens behind those clean walls is another question.
Les Abysses de Velkor: Les Abysses de Velkor descend into darkness. Literally — the station is built into a geological fault, and the deepest levels get no natural light at all. Velkor chose this spot precisely for that reason.

They say Velkor tests the limits of consciousness. Not as a metaphor — concretely, with devices, protocols, subjects. People who come back up from the lower levels sometimes have that slightly off look, as if something in them had been recalibrated.

The corridors of the Abyss widen and narrow according to a logic that doesn't follow standard building codes. Velkor designed the space as an experience in itself. You notice it when you realize your heart rate has changed since you came in.

At level -7, gravity is slightly different. Not enough to fall, but enough that your gait is slightly off. The regulars walk with an adapted ease. You stumble slightly over nothing, and no one asks if you're okay.
L'Académie Stellaire: L'Académie Stellaire is the only place in the sector where people pay to learn. Not practical training — pure knowledge. Archivist Zenn built something that looks more like a temple of information than an educational institution.

The Academy's students look like they've slept little and read a lot. They wander the corridors checking portable terminals, debating in low voices. You feel slightly illiterate in this constant flow of people who seem to know things you'll never know.

The Academy's great library spans five levels. Shelves of physical data — crystals, disks, printed polymer scrolls. Zenn believes physical information lasts better than digital. She cites specific catastrophes. No one contradicts her.

A debate is underway in the main lecture hall. Two people arguing about something you don't fully understand — the ethics of consciousness exploration, maybe, or the historicity of the Great War. The crowd is silent and attentive. Intellectual precision here carries the same intensity as violence does elsewhere.
Les Décombres de Vael: Les Décombres de Vael are all that's left of a space city destroyed during the Great War. The partially collapsed structures were stabilized just enough to avoid catastrophic failure, and people settled into the gaps.
Vael's architecture is a layering. Underneath — elegant, precise, meant to house tens of thousands. On top: improvised constructions, tarps, walkways welded between wrecks. You're walking on history.

An old mural depicts a thriving space city — glowing spires, ships in procession. Half of it is damaged. The remaining colors are vivid enough to show you what it once was. You stay in front of it longer than expected.

The Elder sits in his usual spot, in a salvaged chair that must have thirty years of service in that exact position. He doesn't watch the passersby — he records them. His memory of Vael before the war is the most precious resource left here.

Archaeological digs have been going on in the East sector for two years. A team of five people exhuming what the war buried. They make meticulous gestures over what could be everyday objects, or evidence of something else.
Épave de l'Aurore Noire: L'Aurore Noire was a command cruiser. Two kilometers long, built to last a hundred years, it made it thirty before being hit. The wreck has been drifting ever since. Inside, generations of scavengers have taken what they could. Some sections remain intact.

The inside of L'Aurore Noire is a labyrinth. The original blueprints circulate but are partly wrong — the ship was modified in an emergency during the battle. Scavengers use a chalk-marking system to avoid getting lost. You find old markings. Some have been erased.

In the comms room, the systems are dead but the logs are intact. Messages sent and never received. Orders whose recipients are dead. A last personal message from the captain to an address that no longer exists. You close the terminal.

The officers' quarters of L'Aurore Noire remain in an unusual state — tables, chairs, navigation charts still pinned to the walls. Someone cleaned here recently. There are fresh footprints in the dust. You weren't the first one today.
Le Vaisseau Fantôme Errant: The Wandering Ghost Ship has no official name. It drifts on an elliptical trajectory known for forty years. No one knows who built it, who abandoned it, or why. Theories vary. The facts are simple: the ship is there, empty, and sometimes not quite empty.

Inside the Ghost Ship, there's food. Decades expired, but present. Tables set, glasses placed as if someone were about to return. The quality of preservation is inexplicable given the state of the systems.

Scavengers who've spent time on the Ghost Ship report sounds. Not machinery — the ship has no power. Sounds that resemble distant voices, footsteps in a parallel corridor. The rational ones explain it as thermal warping. The others don't explain it at all.

There's something in the air here — not a smell, not a presence, but a gentle resistance to movement, as if space itself were slightly denser. Physicists have measured it. The readings are normal. The physicists left quickly.
L'Arc Perdu: L'Arc Perdu appears on no current official map. Raphazarus has something to do with that. He doesn't talk about how.

The corridors of L'Arc Perdu are covered in symbols you don't recognize. Some look like dead languages. Others like technical schematics. Raphazarus marked his territory in a way that predates language. Or surpasses it.

There's a library in L'Arc Perdu. Physical texts — paper, plastic, engraved metal. Millennia of documents. Raphazarus wasn't the first to live here. What came before Raphazarus, he didn't destroy. He read it.

The air of L'Arc Perdu is still in a particular way. Not dead — waiting. Like a held breath. You get the feeling that if you made noise now, something very far away in the station would hear it and never forget.
Esmeralda: You land on Esmeralda and the first thing that hits you is the air. Real air, unfiltered, unrecycled, that smells of trees and humidity and something alive that no life-support system has ever managed to reproduce.

The forest of Esmeralda begins right after the arrival structures. Abruptly. A wall of dense, ancient vegetation that's had millennia to decide its own shape without any human interference. King Maxance established strict no-intervention zones.

The markets of Esmeralda sell things impossible to find elsewhere. Spices with no synthetic equivalent. Plant-based textiles that last thirty years. The merchants here don't haggle — prices are fixed, quantities limited.

A creature you couldn't name crosses the street in front of you, indifferent. Large, slow. Esmeralda's residents step aside slightly but without fear. You step aside too. Out of courtesy if not caution.

An artificial rain begins at level 4. Nozzles built into the ceiling release a gentle drizzle at regular intervals — not for agriculture but for well-being. Walking under that warm drizzle in Esmeralda's plant-scented air is the closest thing to a planet you've experienced in a long time.

The kids of Esmeralda play in the forest. Not miniature adult games — games that only exist in this forest, with rules they don't explain to adults. A child watches you from a high branch with a look of assessment that shouldn't belong to someone their age.
Scotty Golden North: Scotty Golden North is a promise of light in the dark of space. The golden signs are visible for kilometers. Inside, everything is designed so you don't check your watch, don't think about tomorrow.

Scotty's casino is organized into zones of increasing intensity. The periphery is soft — light games, free drinks. The deeper you go, the higher the stakes, the lower the noise. At the center, a few private rooms whose doors only open for certain people.

Scotty's dealers are trained in psychology as much as in the rules of the games. They know how to spot when someone's losing more than they should, when the night turns. The most efficient profit machine cares about its clients' health. Up to a point.
Samy Scotty is visible from his balcony almost every hour. He watches. Not out of suspicion — out of fascination. He loves people who gamble. He built this place to watch them. Money is the pretext.

The upper-floor restaurant at Scotty's serves cuisine you can't afford. But you can sit at the bar that runs alongside it and watch the dishes go by. Sometimes someone leaves one untouched and the waiter looks away. It's the only way to get real food here without ten thousand credits.
Star Quest: Star Quest vibrates. The music starts right at the entry airlocks — not aggressive, just present, preparing you for something. Mister Eliotis has a theory about the optimal tempo for welcoming new arrivals. What you're hearing is the result of years of hedonic research.
The party at Eliotis's place isn't continuous — it's perpetual. Different spaces, different moods, different intensities. Cocktails whose names are made-up words serving very specific expectations.

You cross paths with people from every sector in the corridors of Star Quest. Military pilots on leave, merchants celebrating a good deal, criminals celebrating something they can't name publicly. Eliotis welcomes everyone with the same smile.

There's a place in Star Quest called The White Room. Not on the official plans. You reach it through a passage behind the kitchens. What happens there depends on who you are and what Eliotis has decided you deserve.
Emporium Requiem: Emporium Requiem is an artificial planet. The structure was built to resemble a planet — habitable surface, maintained atmosphere, simulated gravity at 0.98g. Walking here means walking on something people built entirely from scratch.
The markets of the Emporium span kilometers. Each level is a specialty — materials, artifacts, information, access. Prices are displayed in gold because credits lack prestige here.

There's a rule at the Emporium no one explains to you at the entrance: courtesy is mandatory. People here settle their disputes through means other than violence, and those other means are often far worse.

The customs office of Emporium Requiem is famous for its calculated inefficiency. The lines are long, the checks thorough, the inspectors slow. It's intentional — delays generate fees, fees get negotiated. That someone isn't you.

At level 9 of the Emporium, where the lighting is dimmer and the signs smaller, are the real markets. The things that can't be displayed at the commercial level. People sitting at café tables looking at their terminals, not looking at you. The most discreet transaction is the most expensive.
La Citadelle Écarlate: La Citadelle Écarlate takes its name from the reddish alloy cladding that covers its outer walls. Grand Guardian Sorath rules this place with a rigor that would be excessive anywhere else. Here it's the norm.

The Scarlet Guardians on patrol have the look of people who believe in something. Not just a job — a mission. Sorath cultivated that deliberately. Faith in order, in protection, in the idea that a line can be held if enough people decide to hold it.

The Citadel's recruit training is visible from the outer walkways. Formations, combat drills, response protocols. It's beautiful in the way precise movement can be beautiful. And slightly terrifying for the same reason.
Fort Ossian: Fort Ossian is a perfectly maintained war machine. General Ossian is obsessed with detail — every piece of equipment checked, every protocol followed. The fort never lets its guard down. Even in peacetime, the alert level stays high enough to go operational in eighty seconds.
The weapons market of Fort Ossian is legal, rigorously documented, and terribly well-stocked. Ossian doesn't allow bad equipment to be sold on his land. He considers it a moral issue.

The soldiers of Fort Ossian eat together at precise hours. Meals are balanced according to nutritional specifications the General validated himself. The food is good. Not delicious — precisely good. Functionally optimal.
Les Puits de Noctis: Les Puits de Noctis descend deep into the rock. The galleries sink to levels where pressure and heat make the work exhausting. Miners work forced rotations because no one would last more than a week straight in the deep levels. Director Pale calculates that rotation is cheaper than replacement.

Natural light never reaches the levels where the miners work. They don't see the sky for weeks. Some eventually stop needing to — their biological cycle adapts. It's a form of adaptation Director Pale actively encourages.

The control office of the Wells is a glass room above level 1. You can see everything that comes in and goes out from there. Director Pale is rarely visible there but his representatives watch constantly. The miners know they're being watched. They've learned to work as if they didn't.

A group of miners coming out of well 7 passes in front of you. Their faces are covered in that particular black dust that doesn't wash off easily. They walk in silence, eyes in the blank stare of someone dreaming with their eyes open. Some of them look very young.
Terminus Sud: Terminus Sud is where things end. The space routes stop here, the maps get vague, the services run out. Yenna, the local informant, knows everything there is to know about what passes through and what doesn't.

The bar of Terminus Sud is the one place everyone eventually passes through. Pilots at the end of the line, merchants whose route got complicated, people looking for one last chance before deciding what to do with their lives. The bartender has heard every story. He repeats none of them.

At Terminus Sud, you can buy routes. Not maps — living routes, with corrupted checkpoints, patrols that look the other way at certain hours, unofficial fuel caches. Yenna sells that. She doesn't invent them. She's been observing them for years.
Station Rocaille: Station Rocaille was built on an asteroid no one planned to inhabit. The first occupants were miners waiting for extraction. The extraction never came. The miners built around themselves. Two generations later, the station is a network of galleries carved into the ore.
The population of Rocaille is tough. Not aggressive — tough. There's a difference. People here don't look for trouble but don't avoid it either. Every hand you shake has calluses.

Little Mara runs a parts market on level 3. Her prices are fair, her warranties real, and she'll tell you to your face if what you want to buy is a mistake. She rules her corner of the station with an authority so natural you forget she was never officially elected to anything.
Avant-Poste Kalem: Avant-Poste Kalem is exactly what its name suggests: an outpost. Small, functional, no wasted space. Commander Voss designed it as an operational base rather than a living station. Even the bar looks like a military mess hall.
The mercenaries recruited by Voss come from everywhere and generally don't stay long. The outpost is a starting point, not a destination. You pass people between two contracts.

A job board hangs at the entrance to Voss's office. Commercial offensives disguised as security, escorts that look like invasions, 'recoveries' of property whose legitimacy is questionable. The pay is good. Questions aren't encouraged.
La Forge des Damnés: La Forge des Damnés produces weapons no official catalog lists. Armorer Skade works to order, to spec, no questions. Her weapons carry no serial numbers. That's not a flaw — it's a feature.

The workers of the Forge aren't all here by choice. Some have debts, some have families someone is watching. You can read it in their movements — precise, efficient, and completely automatic. People whose will has been removed through pressure.
The Forge's sales floor is austere — weapons on display racks, prices posted, no one doing active selling. You choose, you pay, you leave. Skade believes good weapons sell themselves. Hers do.
Port Méridien: Port Méridien smells clean. An artificial clean — filtration systems that mask something else. Guards in neutral uniforms who smile without it reaching their eyes. The most legal commercial hub in the sector, which doesn't mean much.

The crowd at Port Méridien is dense and quiet for its size. Merchants have learned not to shout prices here — the station's image demands a certain restraint. Transactions happen in low voices, smiles stay calibrated, prices stay insulting.
Lit signs, wide corridors, shops that give the illusion of a planet. Port Méridien was designed to make you forget you're in space. It almost works. Except when you look out the portholes.

A security agent has been following you since the entrance. He's discreet — professional. He's not looking for a pretext. He's looking for certainty. At Port Méridien, strangers get a grace period. You're still in yours.
Le Nid des Faucons: Le Nid des Faucons is clean. Military clean — not a speck of dust, not a misplaced cable. It's not pride, it's discipline. Someone inspects these corridors regularly. Someone notes what's out of the ordinary.

The Black Hawks on duty watch you arrive from their posts. Not with suspicion — with cold assessment. Within ten seconds, each of them has decided what they'd do if you became a problem. You feel the conclusion in their eyes before they look away.

The Black Hawks' emblem is everywhere here — carved into the walls, embroidered on uniforms, painted in black on the floor of the central hall. It's not a mark, it's a statement. Alanossa built this place so it wouldn't be forgotten.
A particular silence reigns at Le Nid des Faucons. Not the absence of sound — machines run, voices speak — but the absence of idle chatter. Every word has a purpose here. Yours will need one too.
La Forge Noire: The air of La Forge Noire is thick — heated metal, burnt lubricant, the particular smoke of alloys that shouldn't be worked. Industrial fans try to filter it. They do what they can.

Rook is somewhere in the workshops — you hear him before you see him. A hammer on an anvil, steady as a heartbeat. La Forge Noire revolves around that rhythm. Everything else organizes around production.

The weapons displayed in the main corridor carry no labels. No names, no codes, no serial numbers. La Forge Noire sells what it makes to those who know what they want. If you have to ask, you're probably not the right customer.

Workers pass without looking at you, carrying parts from one workshop to another. Their movements are precise, economical. La Forge Noire doesn't tolerate wasted time. Even visitors end up walking faster.
L'Entrepôt Zéro: L'Entrepôt Zéro hasn't had an official owner for long enough that the question no longer comes up. People use it. Things pass through it. Deals get struck in corridors that have no name.
Crates stacked to the ceiling in some sectors, sections empty for so long someone set up a makeshift camp in them. L'Entrepôt Zéro became a city by accident. No one voted for this outcome.

Security at L'Entrepôt Zéro works through a balance of interests — too many people have something to lose here for any one group to take control. It holds. It's held for long enough that residents have stopped asking how much longer.
Someone put up a sign at the main entrance. It just says 'ZERO'. Below it, someone else added 'EXACTLY'. That's the only philosophy of the place.
Le Perchoir: Le Perchoir is exactly what its name suggests: a high point to watch from. Cameras everywhere, guards at every angle, and the sense that everyone's already been catalogued before they even walk in.
The asteroid vibrates slightly underfoot — stabilization thrusters constantly compensating. The Black Hawks built this post to last, not to be comfortable.
A Black Hawk on duty watches you from the control post. He says nothing. He takes notes. Everyone who comes in here gets noted.
Station Ombre: Station Ombre doesn't exist on the official maps. You're therefore officially nowhere, which is a strangely liberating thought — until you realize what that means for your safety.
The corridors of Station Ombre are lit in dim red. Not for atmosphere — so the cameras work better in the infrared spectrum. You understand this after a few minutes.
Black Hawk operators work in silence at terminals whose screens are angled so you can't read them. The information flowing here isn't for you.
Relais Noir: Le Relais Noir smells of fuel and efficiency. No one comes here to linger — you come to refuel, deliver, and leave. The Black Hawks designed this place so transactions happen fast.
Technicians in gray uniforms work on docked ships in professional silence. They don't ask questions. You won't either.
A screen above the entrance displays rates. Fuel, ammunition, rations. No haggling. No credit. Cash payment only.
La Tanière: La Tanière has several layers — like its occupants. On the surface, the signs of a former military base. Underneath, modifications only pirates would have thought to make. Alanossa kept both.
Combat trophies decorate the corridors — not like a museum, like a warning. Some belong to factions that still exist. They know their emblems are here.
The atmosphere here is thick in a way that has nothing to do with the ventilation systems. It's the pressure of people who have everything to lose and decided it no longer mattered.
Fort de Cendres: Fort de Cendres owes its name to what was here before — an outpost that burned in a conflict no one talks about anymore. The Black Hawks built on top of it. The black walls absorb everything.
Black Hawk recruits training in the inner courtyard don't notice your arrival. They've learned to notice only what they're told to notice.
The efficiency here is meticulous. Everything in its place, everyone in their role. Alanossa imposed this rigor. Fort de Cendres is its purest expression.
L'Œil du Faucon: From L'Œil du Faucon, you can see several sectors at once. Steerable antennas cover the entire outer hull. Analysts process data continuously. Someone here knows what you did last week.
Lyss is at her usual post, surrounded by screens. She doesn't look up when you enter. She's already had your silhouette in her sensors since you approached the perimeter.
The silence of L'Œil is the silence of total concentration. People listening to everything that passes without ever transmitting themselves. You wonder what they've heard about you.
Repaire Vega-Sud: If the Undercroft has a basement, it's Repaire Vega-Sud. What's too visible up there lands here. The people who live here have made choices even the Undercroft's residents find questionable.
The smell here is different from Vega — more concentrated, more chemical. Synthetic byproducts linger in the air. The vents aren't doing their job, or they're doing it on purpose.
Mako behind his counter watches you with no expression. He's seen every kind of customer. He's developed a philosophy: what you want is your problem. What you can pay is his.
Bastion Mineur: Le Bastion Mineur looks like a miniature Citadel — same codes, same colors, same seriousness. That's intentional. The Guardians believe in consistency of image.
Harek patrols his post with the precision of someone who's turned routine into an art form. Eight years in this bastion. He knows every joint, every shadow, every abnormal sound.
A plaque on the wall lists the names of the Guardians who've served here since it opened. Some have been removed. The plaque doesn't say why.
Poste Vigie: Poste Vigie is the quietest place in Guardian territory. Two soldiers. A spyglass. A radio signal. And Sera, who writes everything in a journal no one else reads.

The view from Poste Vigie's portholes covers an entire space corridor. Sera can tell you exactly how many ships have passed through here in the last six months. She knows it without checking her notes.
Boredom here is structural. The Guardians built it into the post's profile. Those who stay develop either extraordinary patience, or something else.
L'Arsenal Écarlate: L'Arsenal Écarlate smells of clean metal and maintenance oil. Every weapon here is maintained, catalogued, calibrated. Drav knows the serial number of every one of them.
Ammunition crates in perfect rows. Armor on rotating displays. L'Arsenal Écarlate is the physical catalog of the Guardians' power.
Drav watches you as if you were working on something — even if you're not working on anything. He judges people by how they look at his weapons. You don't yet know what he's concluded.
La Forteresse Exilée: La Forteresse Exilée kept the Guardians' walls but not their spirit. Something else has moved in instead — fewer rules, more resentment.
Keln moves through these corridors as if he'd known them since childhood — because in a way, he has. He served in this fort before. He wasn't supposed to come back.
The Guardians' emblems have been partly erased from the walls. Only partly. Keln left the traces. A reminder of what he lost, or what he chose to lose.
Comptoir Sud: Comptoir Sud is the Emporium on a smaller budget — less shine, more accessibility. Mira behind her counter smiles the same way as her colleagues on the upper level, but the smile is slightly less rehearsed.
The goods here are decent quality. Not the rare items from the main commercial level — those stay up there. But an honest range for quick transactions.
Deals close here every ten minutes on average. Mira counted. She counts everything, actually.
Annexe Commerciale: L'Annexe Commerciale is where the Emporium shows its most presentable face. Clean corridors, discreet staff, an atmosphere resembling a private bank.
Rexx greets you with a professional precision that makes it feel like your visit was planned long in advance. He's worked in this environment long enough that the facade has become natural.
Meetings take place in glass rooms you can see but not hear. People in tailored outfits around smooth tables. What's being decided here probably involves large sums.
Relais de Transit: Le Relais de Transit is the Emporium's hidden mechanism — the place where logistics flows get organized before becoming visible. Olin knows the movement of every crate.
Automated carts move in precise patterns. Technicians check manifests. Efficiency here is functional, not aesthetic.
A section of the Relais is hermetically sealed. Olin will tell you it's maintenance. He'll sound sincere. He's probably sincere.
Résidence Orbitale: La Résidence Orbitale offers something nowhere else in the sector can: quiet. A quiet that's been acquired, preserved, and billed accordingly.
Lady Sonn watches you from the common lounge with the calm of someone with nothing left to prove to anyone. Thirty years in this residence. She's seen many leave. She stays.
The rooms of the Résidence have real portholes, not screens. Looking at space from here is a different experience — no alarms, no ship noise, just the void, waiting.
Club Privé Éos: Le Club Privé Éos has no sign. Those who need to know where it is know. Those who don't aren't meant to enter.
Sael greets you with perfect neutrality that says more than any expression could. In this club, the host sees everything and reveals nothing. That's what he's paid for.
Conversations happen in groups of two or three in separate alcoves. The background music is calibrated to cover exactly the range of a normal voice. Nothing here is accidental.
Les Cendres: Les Cendres still smell of burning, twenty years later. The filtration systems can't remove it — either they're not powerful enough, or someone prefers it stays.
Murn looks at you like someone who's learned to quickly assess whether a person will be a problem. He was there when it burned. He survived something he doesn't describe. It shows.
Whole sections are sealed off — not because they're dangerous, but because no one has the resources to restore them. And because some prefer not to see what's behind them.
Station Quarantaine: The quarantine is officially lifted. The atmosphere doesn't seem to have gotten the message. Something in the air of this station causes a faint nausea — or it's your imagination.
Docta receives you in her infirmary with the calm of someone who's treated cases the manuals don't cover. She doesn't ask about your health. She observes and takes notes.
The residents of Station Quarantaine have that particular look of people who went through something together and don't need to explain it to others. An unspoken code. You're outside that code.
Le Berceau: Le Berceau is older than any current conflict. Its walls carry construction systems no one manufactures anymore — technologies whose blueprints were lost or destroyed.
Archivist Zal watches you enter with the patience of someone who's been waiting a long time. He keeps archives. He knows things. The question is what he's willing to share.

Something about the gravity of Le Berceau is slightly different — not enough to affect movement, but enough for the body to notice after a few hours. An anomaly the scientists who came to measure it never explained.
L'Épave Vivante: L'Épave Vivante has its own levels now — improvised levels within what used to be a cargo ship's structure. Cables run in directions that match no original blueprint.
Captain Oss moves through his wreck with the confidence of someone at home — because he is, literally. His ship became his city. He stopped making the distinction.
Families have lived here for two generations. Their children were born in the converted holds and know these corridors better than any blueprint. They are the blueprint.
Station Fantôme: Station Fantôme has been broadcasting a navigation signal for ten years. The signal says the station is empty. The signal is technically a lie.
Shel saw you coming long before you cleared the entry airlock. She lets you in because she decided you could come in. That's an important distinction here.
The residents of Station Fantôme have developed an economy of the invisible — they produce nothing that can be traced, trade nothing that can be tracked. They exist in the margins of the margins.
L'Oasis de Fer: L'Oasis de Fer is the only place in the sector where representatives of rival factions cross paths without shooting each other. The agreement that maintains this peace is oral, unwritten, and respected by all — because everyone has something to lose.
Tonn manages this balance with the precision of a diplomat and the bluntness of a soldier. He personally negotiated the terms of neutrality with each faction. He never reveals the details.
Merchants, mercenaries, faction agents sitting at the same tables. No one talks about their affiliation. No one needs to.
La Balise: La Balise pulses. A steady signal that's guided pilots in the sector for forty years. Rinn maintains that signal with a care others reserve for living things.
From La Balise, you can hear all the sector's radio traffic if you know how to tune the frequencies. Rinn knows how. She's been listening for years. She notes what seems important to her.

La Balise's crew is small — five people who take turns maintaining the signal. They've developed their own culture, rituals around the signal, a way of being together visitors don't always understand.
Confluent: Confluent is where the routes converge — not by chance, by design. Someone, long ago, calculated the exact intersection of the most-used trade corridors and put a station there.
Broxx knows the current prices of forty stations. He'll tell you straight if you ask. He sells that information as much as his goods.
The population of Confluent turns over constantly. Permanent residents, but mostly people passing through. Every day brings new faces. Broxx remembers them all.
Port de Nuit: Port de Nuit has no day — the lighting stays constant at an intensity resembling a perpetual evening. It's an aesthetic choice that's also practical: no one sees clearly what's changing hands.
The Queen of Night controls this port from a table in the darkest corner of the main bar. She rarely stands up. It's not necessary — everyone comes to her.
Transactions at Port de Nuit follow an unwritten but strict etiquette. Some things aren't said aloud. Some names aren't spoken. Violations are noted.
Station Zéphyr: Station Zéphyr floats in the atmospheric zone of a gas giant — high enough to be safe, low enough for the research sensors to work. The researchers have learned to ignore the turbulence.
Dr. Vael is in his data, as always. He's been searching for something in the atmospheric compositions for twelve years. He hasn't found it yet. He hasn't stopped looking either.
The windows of Station Zéphyr look out on planet-sized clouds in constant motion. It's both beautiful and profoundly inhospitable. The researchers stopped noticing.
L'Observatoire: L'Observatoire is four hours' flight from the nearest station. That's intentional. Elenne chose this location precisely for its isolation — less light pollution, fewer stray vibrations.
Elenne spends her days watching stars no one else watches. She notes what she sees in journals no one else reads. She's at peace with that.
The silence of L'Observatoire is the most complete silence you've ever known in space. Something in that silence has a texture — as if the absence of sound were itself information.
Station Limite: Station Limite is the last point on the map. Beyond it, data becomes sparse, then nonexistent. Kaed is one of the few who's pushed further. He only talks about it to those who ask the right question.
The equipment at Station Limite shows the signs of constant use in extreme conditions. Everything is functional. Nothing is beautiful. That's the philosophy of the frontier.
Pilots stop here before continuing into the unknown. Some come back. Some send a signal from very far away. Some stop sending word at all. Kaed keeps a list.
Les Cavernes de Mira: Les Cavernes de Mira go deeper into the asteroid than any map shows. The miners know levels that don't officially exist.
Grelm runs the operations with the efficiency of someone who's learned survival depends on organization. He took the position under circumstances rarely discussed. The miners follow him.

In the deep levels of the Caves, the pressure changes. Sounds travel differently. The miners who've worked there a long time have habits, rituals, a way of interacting with the rock newcomers don't understand.
La Raffinerie: La Raffinerie is always hot. The thermal systems manage the excess heat from the refining process but never fully neutralize it. You get used to it, the workers say. It's true in an unsettling way.
Brenn coordinates the crews with a minimum of words. Everyone here knows what they have to do — repeating instructions would be an insult. La Raffinerie runs like a well-oiled organism.
Columns of refined fuel wait in pressurized tanks. The value of what passes through here every week is astronomical. The security measures are proportional.
La Couronne d'Eos: La Couronne d'Eos hangs above everything else — a high orbital station looking down at the others from a distance. Its corridors are wide, its ceilings high, its surfaces clean in a way that costs money. A lot of money. The kind you stop counting.

The people who come to La Couronne d'Eos don't carry their own bags. They don't wait in line either. They arrive, someone's expecting them, things get handled. You're probably the only one here who checked the price of fuel before coming.

Conversations happen in low voices in closed lounges. Decisions affecting thousands of people get made here between two flutes of something imported. La Couronne d'Eos doesn't look like a place where power is exercised. That's exactly why it is one.

An advisor watches you from the other side of a glass corridor. He sizes you up with the precision of someone who's spent his life assessing what others are worth. You couldn't say whether you passed the test. He leaves before you decide to ask him.
